newsitem.title: BELGIUM: NATO agrees to stabilisation force in Bosnia.
newsitem.headline: NATO agrees to stabilisation force in Bosnia.

text.p: NATO foreign ministers, striving to achieve stability in Bosnia, formally approved a plan on Tuesday to send between 25,000 and 30,000 troops to monitor the Balkan state's peace accords next year.
The 16 ministers agreed that a stabilisation force (SFOR) should replace the current alliance-led implementation force (IFOR) when its mandate expires on December 20.

"From now on, the destiny of the Bosnians will be more and more in their own hands," French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette said in his opening speech to a two-day meeting of NATO allies in Brussels.
"The measuring board for our success will be how to achieve durable self-perpetuating stability," German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel told a news conference after the accord was struck.

Under the follow-on arrangement, signed just over a year after the signing of the Dayton Peace accords, the soldiers' mandate will be changed slightly to assist the development of civilian institutions rather than to enforce the accord.
The force will be used to support municipal elections which are expected to be held in April.

Under the plan, Germany, mindful of a European Union drive to forge a common defence identity, will participate on the ground as part of a Franco-German brigade for the first time since before World War One.
A German major-general will be chief of staff for the force and will take up his post in the New Year in the Sarajevo headquarters of the SFOR.

Germany's role in any peacekeeping force in the Balkans has long been a controversial issue, both in domestic political terms and internationally because of Nazi Germany's World War Two occupation and its vicious fight against local partisans.

The new force, which will be endorsed by a U.N. Security Council resolution next week, will remain in Bosnia for 18 months with reviews every six months and be progressively reduced as the mission's expiry date approaches.

Seventeen non-NATO countries, including Russia, which are taking part in the IFOR mission, which was sent in to oversee implementation of last year's Dayton peace accords, have agreed to participate in SFOR.
NATO hopes the cooperation will help it build better relations with former enemies it will not invite to join the alliance at a special summit in July next year.

In a speech to fellow ministers, U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher underlined the need for "new and effective approaches" to apprehend the many indicted war criminals still at large in Bosnia.

State Department Spokesman Nicholas Burns, asked how this could be done, said more support could be given to the Hague war crimes tribunal and more pressure put on the parties to the Dayton Accord to hand over suspects on their territory.

IFOR, under instructions to detain only suspects who fall into its hands, has not carried out any arrests and U.S. officials have given no indication that the instructions given to SFOR will be any different.
